ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Latin -tō Latin cessōder. Middle French cesserbor. Middle English cesen English cease From Middle English cesen, cessen, from Middle French cesser (“to cease”), from Latin cessō (“leave off”), frequentative of cēdō (“to leave off, go away”). Compare secede.

ex: And with that, his twitching ceased.
After a short while, it ceased to rain.
And with that, he ceased twitching.

senses.d: To be wanting; to fail; to pass away, perish.
ex: The poor shall never cease out of the land.
[...] wherefore ceaſe we then? / Say they who counſel Warr, we are decreed, / Reſerv'd and deſtin'd to Eternal woe;

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French cesser, from Old French cesser, borrowed from Latin cessāre.

it:cessare.gl: to stop, to finish, to cease

it:arrestare.gl: to halt, to stop, to check, to staunch

ety.text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō, restāre (“stop, remain behind, stay back”).
Borrowed from Latin cessāre, whence also Spanish cejar (“forfeit”).
